pages.description: Why we built Tensorcraft, how it maps ML onto JavaScript, and what we deliberately left out.

contentExcerpts.label: Publisher and teaching method
contentExcerpts.text: ABOUTWhy this course exists.We’re a group of JavaScript engineers who wanted to learn ML through code we already understood. We built Tensorcraft to make that possible.The lessons start with familiar code: useState helps introduce the idea of changing model state, Array.reduce can calculate a neuron’s weighted sum, and Math.max(0, x) is ReLU for a single number.Each comparison explains how far it holds. Some are exact, like ReLU. Others share a structure or offer a way to picture the idea. We label those differences and explain where an analogy stops working.Exercises run your code and check what it does. 65 exercises are live today. They run in a browser worker with TensorFlow.js available, and we check their reference solutions in CI. We have written 300 exercises across the five planned worlds. We have completed release checks for the published exercises. Some use tensors and models directly. Others cover the data preparation, validation, and deployment code around them.We plan five worlds (Deep Orbit, Neon Protocol, Signal Ward, Nova Canvas, Terra Grid), each with its own story and ML curriculum. Deep Orbit is the one open today. Across its modules you assemble a working browse

pages.title: TensorFlow.js reshape vs transpose, Tensorcraft
pages.description: Compare reshape and transpose in TensorFlow.js with exact outputs, runnable JavaScript, and a sensor-data example for JavaScript developers.
headings: Shape alone cannot identify a sensor

contentExcerpts.label: Direct technical answer
contentExcerpts.text: TensorcraftGuidesTensorFlow.js reshape vs transposereshape() changes a tensor's shape while keeping its flattened values in order. transpose() permutes its axes. For a two-dimensional tensor, the default transpose exchanges rows and columns.By Tensorcraft, a group of JavaScript engineers. Updated November 10, 2026. Example verified with TensorFlow.js 4.22.0.One sensor's readings over timeIn Deep Orbit, the crew investigates an unexplained signal. Farah selects sensors A, B, C, and D from Demir's fictional 64-sensor recording. The excerpt below contains those four sensors at three local moments. It uses the same data as the free tensor-shapes

contentExcerpts.label: Runnable example
contentExcerpts.text: The runnable TensorFlow.js exampleInstall the pinned runtime with npm install @tensorflow/tfjs@4.22.0. Save the following code as compare.mjs and run node compare.mjs. A browser project can use the same module through its bundler.import * as tf from "@tensorflow/tfjs"; await tf.ready(); // Local moments 0, 1, 2. Sensor order: A, B, C, D. const packet = [ [ 2, 20, 5, 8 ], [ 3, 18, 7, 8 ], [ 4, 16, 6, 9 ] ]; const comparison = tf.tidy(() => { const input = tf.tensor2d(packet); return { reshaped: input.reshape([4, 3]).arraySync(), transposed: input.transpose().arraySync(), }; }); console.log(comparison);The callback returns ordinary JavaScript arrays from arraySync(). tf.tidy() disposes the tensors created inside that callback because the result contains no tensors. If you return a tensor instead, you keep responsibility for disposing it when you finish using it.This small example uses synchronous reads so you can inspect the values directly. Reading tensor data synchronously can block the browser while a backend finishes its work. Larger applications can use asynchronous reads and dispose tensors explicitly afterward. tf.tidy() requires a synchronous callback.Shape alone cannot identify a sensorA shape such as [4, 3] tells you dimension sizes. The recording header supplies the sensor order and moment order. contentExcerpts.text: Shape alone cannot identify a sensorA shape such as [4, 3] tells you dimension sizes. The recording header supplies the sensor order and moment order. contentExcerpts.label: Task and data provenance
contentExcerpts.text: TensorcraftGuidesA browser ML project: a rule, a model, and a recorded mistakeA useful ML project compares a trained model with a simple baseline, inspects mistakes, and runs the saved result in an application. Deep Orbit's independent project asks you to do that with recorded room measurements and JavaScript.By Tensorcraft, a group of JavaScript engineers. Updated November 10, 2026.The task and its dataA facilities team wants a review-only display of whether one office is occupied. The inputs are temperature, relative humidity, light, CO₂, and humidity ratio. You choose features, chronological training/validation/test periods, error costs, a model, and a decision threshold.The starter includes 2,056 recorded measurements derived from the UCI Occupancy Detection dataset. These are real room recordings. They are a separate source from Deep Orbit's fictional ship data.Tensorcraft sorted the source's 20,560 readings by timestamp and kept every tenth row. The subset preserves values and labels. This sampling reduces download size. It does not make nearby observations independent. The source timestamps have no assigned timezone.The data attribution and modification record supplies the citation, CC BY 4.0 terms, archive hash, and transformation details. The experiment serves one recorded room. It does not establish performance in another building or suitability for access controls.One validation reading where both policies were wrongThis supplied score comes from our recorded demon

contentExcerpts.label: Demonstration scope
contentExcerpts.text: What the demonstration establishesThe example above comes from a maintainer integration fixture, recorded 2026-09-19 with TensorFlow.js 4.22.0 on its cpu backend. Five fixed training epochs checked the saved-model workflow. This is supplied demonstration work, separate from a learner's project.The model and the light-threshold rule both classify this validation reading as occupied at the recorded settings. Its label says unoccupied. Their agreement does not establish correctness. One row also cannot establish either policy's overall quality.You can inspect the exact reading, score, artifact hashes, fixture hash and reproduction commands in the recorded fixture. The recorded hashes identify the demonstration artifacts. The starter download contains no trained solution.Your work and the supplied toolsResponsibilities in the independent projectYou createThe starter suppliesFeature choices, data periods, baseline and training experimentRecorded data, attribution and a training-file skeletonSaved model, preprocessing parameters and evaluation runsExport/reload helpers and metric arithmeti

contentExcerpts.label: Evaluation
contentExcerpts.text: An honest evaluationFit preprocessing with training rows. Use validation data to choose model settings and thresholds. Freeze those choices before evaluating the final test period. If you change the policy after inspecting that period, it becomes development data and you need new data for an independent test.Compare the rule and model on the same rows, inspect false positives and missed occupancy, and include your chosen error costs. Keeping the rule is a valid outcome when it serves the task better.Automated checks can detect overlapping row IDs and recompute scores. They cannot prove that you avoided looking at the final period or that your reasoning is sound.
